question:
Patient note:
A 61-year-old man with a background of degenerative knee osteoarthritis controlled intermittently with over-the-counter naproxen 500 mg twice daily, mild diet-controlled type 2 diabetes, and uncomplicated hyperlipidemia managed on rosuvastatin presented to the emergency department at 09:20 after noting two consecutive coal-black, viscous bowel movements during the early morning hours that coated the waterline, emitted a pungent metallic odor, and required repeated wipes before the tissue appeared gray. He denied vomiting, retching, coughing blood, coffee-ground material, fresh hematochezia, or crimson streaking on the toilet paper. He reported a four-day history of gnawing epigastric discomfort worse when his stomach was empty and temporarily relieved by a glass of milk or an antacid tablet; the pain did not radiate, was unassociated with exertion, and had no accompanying diaphoresis. He specifically stated that at no point did his vision tunnel, the room spin, or his knees buckle, and he remained fully upright walking from the bedroom to the bathroom without losing awareness. There were no complaints of chest pressure, palpitations, paroxysmal dyspnea, ankle swelling, fever, chills, night sweats, or unintended weight loss. His surgical history is limited to a remote right inguinal hernia repair, and he has never undergone endoscopic evaluation of the upper gastrointestinal tract. He consumes one to two light beers on weekends, quit smoking nineteen years ago after a ten-pack-year habit, and denies illicit substance use. He has never been told he has viral, alcoholic, or metabolic liver disease, has no history of jaundice or ascites, and his most recent comprehensive metabolic panel six months ago was reportedly normal. Medications consist of rosuvastatin 10 mg nightly, metformin 500 mg with dinner, and the aforementioned non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug; he takes no aspirin, clopidogrel, anticoagulants, glucocorticoids, or proton-pump inhibitors. Family history reveals a father with coronary artery disease and a mother with rheumatoid arthritis, but no relatives with peptic ulcer disease or bleeding diathesis. On arrival—before placement of intravenous lines, administration of crystalloid, antiemetics, acid suppressive therapy, vasoactive agents, or blood products—he sat upright on the stretcher appearing apprehensive yet conversant, skin color pale-pink but warm and dry. Manual vital signs measured in the right arm at heart level recorded a blood pressure of 131/78 mm Hg, a regular radial pulse of 75 beats per minute confirmed on three-lead telemetry, respiratory rate 16/min, oral temperature 36.5 °C, and room-air oxygen saturation 98 %. Capillary refill was two seconds; conjunctivae were slightly blanched, sclerae anicteric, and oral mucous membranes moist without telangiectasias. Neck veins were flat at 45°, carotid pulses were brisk without bruits, and peripheral pulses were 2+ symmetric. Cardiac examination revealed distinct S1 and S2 without murmurs, rubs, or gallops. Lungs were clear to auscultation throughout. The abdomen was flat and nondistended; gentle palpation elicited mild tenderness in the epigastrium without guarding, rebound, palpable masses, hepatosplenomegaly, or succussion splash. Bowel sounds were hyperactive. Skin survey showed no spider angiomata, palmar erythema, petechiae, or ecchymoses. A focused neurologic screen demonstrated an alert man oriented to person, place, time, and situation with intact cranial nerves, full motor strength, and steady rapid alternating movements. Digital rectal examination produced a generous smear of jet-black, tarry stool that turned the guaiac card dark blue almost immediately. A single 18-gauge peripheral catheter was inserted solely for laboratory sampling, and before any therapeutic infusion the initial studies returned: hemoglobin 14.3 g/dL, hematocrit 41 %, mean corpuscular volume 89 fL, platelet count 235 × 10⁹/L, white blood cell count 8.4 × 10⁹/L, blood urea nitrogen 62 mg/dL, serum creatinine 0.9 mg/dL (baseline 0.9), sodium 139 mmol/L, potassium 4.1 mmol/L, chloride 104 mmol/L, bicarbonate 23 mmol/L, glucose 112 mg/dL, total bilirubin 0.8 mg/dL, alanine aminotransferase 35 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 32 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 88 U/L, albumin 4.2 g/dL, and international normalized ratio 1.03. A 12-lead electrocardiogram recorded concurrently demonstrated normal sinus rhythm at 76 bpm with normal intervals and no ischemic changes. Portable upright chest radiography showed clear lung fields and a normal cardiomediastinal silhouette, and a single supine abdominal film revealed a nonspecific bowel gas pattern without free intraperitoneal air. The patient remained nil per os, was connected to continuous cardiorespiratory monitoring, and a type-and-screen was dispatched while the on-call gastroenterology service was contacted for expedited esophagogastroduodenoscopy to locate and treat the presumed upper source of his tarry gastrointestinal blood loss.

Question: What is the patient's Glasgow-Blatchford Bleeding score? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
Glasgow-Blatchford Bleeding Score, using pretreatment findings:
- Blood urea: BUN 62 mg/dL × 0.357 = 22.1 mmol/L urea, in the 10 to <25 mmol/L band → 4.
- Hemoglobin: 14.3 g/dL in a man (≥13) → 0.
- Systolic BP: 131 mmHg (≥110) → 0.
- Pulse: 75/min (<100) → 0.
- Melena: black, tarry stool confirmed on rectal examination → 1.
- Syncope: denied → 0.
- Hepatic disease: absent → 0.
- Cardiac failure: absent → 0.
Sum = 4 + 0 + 0 + 0 + 1 + 0 + 0 + 0 = 5.
Final answer: 5
